title: Who's Asking? Identity Delegation for AI Agents and Service Meshes
summary: How Block uses User Identity Delegation to keep the user and the acting software visible, so services can answer who's asking and what's allowed.
body_text: When a request reaches a service, it should be able to answer two questions: who are you, and are you allowed to do this? In a small system, that answer is mostly straightforward. A human signs in through their corporate identity provider, clicks a button to take an action, and a server consults a written policy: is this person allowed to do that action on this resource? The sign-in answers the first question, and the service-owned policy answers the second. We make two assumptions: that the human's identity was verified before onboarding, and the policy came from a trusted source, which is true for services owning their own policies. Then we add modern software engineering. An engineer responding to an incident might ask an agent, "What's going on?" The agent may check telemetry, review recent deploys, search Slack or email, open a change, and deploy a fix. The harness might run locally or in a shared cloud environment. Every system it touches still needs to answer the same questions: who is asking, and what are they allowed to do? If the agent runs as a shared service or harness, many people can send work through the same underlying compute. In that model, we cannot rely only on the agent's backend service identity. That service identity would need enough capabilities to act for everyone. Future users could then inherit those capabilities through agent interactions. That weakens protection against data leakage and unauthorized access, and moves us further away from least-privileged access. If we flip the narrative and have the agent service simply assume the human identity, we have a different problem. We lose control over how systems with different security properties handle potentially sensitive data. Perhaps your telemetry stack contains data you haven't authorized for consumption by a third-party model provider, or users don't feel comfortable providing access to their Slack history. Similar to the agent service identity case, context and how we handle it matters. Both implementations only half answer the "who" of it all. The "are you allowed?" question is muddled because "allowed" depends on a clear "who" taking the action. At Block, we designed a system to give us deeper insight into that "who" so we can better answer whether an action should be allowed. We call it User Identity Delegation. User Identity Delegation gives downstream services a better answer than "the user" or "the agent." It lets a service evaluate: this user, through this software actor acting on their behalf, with this bounded delegated authority, for this request. To understand why User Identity Delegation is necessary, we have to rethink how we talk about software acting on behalf of people. Intentional Anthropomorphism Central to our work around User Identity Delegation is the same question that was our guidepost before widespread agent use: how do we ensure that the right people get access to the right data at the right time in the right place? Agentic AI is not unique in its risk. Agents are units of computation that execute some operation and are called to action by a human or another service. What is unique about agentic adoption is the speed at which access can escalate. Least-privileged access is already a perennial struggle, and agentic velocity makes permission creep easier. Where a command line tool or an application is bounded by its design parameters, agents are intentionally more open-ended. When an agent receives a task and the appropriate authorizations, it will find a way to complete that task, potentially with undesirable side effects. The agent may be enthusiastic, but that enthusiasm is precisely why it cannot be the authorization model. Agents are also naturally seen as extensions of their users. People expect that agents should be able to do all of the same work that they can do, just faster or in parallel. This is, after all, their value proposition. From this model, delegation naturally emerges: a user delegates a task to their agent, and the agent acts on behalf of that user. In the same way that you might delegate the delivery of your pizza to your local pizza delivery driver, you might delegate a task to your agent. When you place the order, the driver does not become you. They get limited authority to do specific work on your behalf: pick up this pizza, use this delivery address, and complete the delivery during a bounded window. Different systems can evaluate different parts of that delegation. At the pizza shop, the decision is about pickup: Subject: you, the person who placed the order Actor: the driver Capability: pick up Resource: pizza order Delegated authority: pick up the order you placed Decision point: the shop counter At the address lookup or delivery step, the decision is different: Subject: you, the person receiving the delivery Actor: the driver Capability: use delivery address Resource: your address Delegated authority: use the address only to complete this delivery Decision point: address lookup or doorstep delivery These boundaries are what make pizza delivery feel reasonable. The driver can act for you because you initiated the order. Their authority applies only to this delivery, only for the address needed to complete it, and only during the delivery window. They have delegated authority, not your full identity. You do not expect the driver to spontaneously deliver you a pizza when you did not ask for it, and you do not expect them to use your address to sign you up for cat fact mailers. User Identity Delegation brings that same shape into software. It preserves who is being represented, what software is acting, what authority was delegated, and whether the requested action is allowed now. The vocabulary we use for this is: Subject: the user whose authority is involved. Actor: the workload, application, CLI, or service harness doing the work. Capability: a named permission that can be evaluated by a downstream service. Delegated authority: the subset of authority the actor is allowed to use. Decision point: the service boundary where the request is evaluated. What We Built User Identity Delegation has four components: Component Job Edge user identity issuer Gets trusted user context into the system at the security boundary. Token exchange Turns short-lived user context into delegated tokens for work that outlives one request. Consent control plane Records what authority a user agreed to delegate to a specific actor, separate from the issuer because consent is user intent rather than authentication. Authorization data plane Validates tokens at decision time and resolves the effective delegated capability set. These pieces exist because neither "the service is calling" nor "the user is calling" is enough context for delegated work. The user has to stay visible, because hiding the user behind a service identity pushes systems toward broad standing access. The actor also has to stay visible, because hiding software behind a user identity makes auditing weaker and makes it harder for downstream services to apply different policy to direct user actions and delegated software actions. The easiest way to see how the components fit together is to follow one request: an internal CLI or agent-backed tool calling a downstream service on behalf of an engineer. One Request Through User Identity Delegation Return to the incident response flow from the opening. An engineer asks an agent-backed tool "What's going on?" The tool needs to read telemetry, search recent deploys, inspect service ownership, and eventually call a downstream service that returns data based on the engineer's permissions. The interesting moment is not the engineer's first prompt; it is the downstream service call after the tool has gathered context and needs data scoped to the engineer's permissions. That downstream service should not just see "the agent service" and it should not just see "the engineer" with no actor context. It should see this engineer, through this software actor acting on their behalf, with bounded authority, for this specific request. The request looks roughly like this: Figure 1: A synchronous request carries the signed user identity JWT to the downstream service, which validates it with the authorization data plane before applying its own policy. The important part is not that every request has this exact shape. The important part is that User Identity Delegation keeps the subject and actor visible at the service boundary, and gives the downstream service a capability set constrained by both current authority and delegated consent. This synchronous path is the first step toward that: it carries verified user context so the service sees the actual user and their current capabilities, while actor attribution and consent clamping arrive with the token exchange. A Request Starts With Verified User Context The engineer starts from an authenticated environment, and at our security boundary the issuer mints a short-lived, signed JWT containing verified user context from that session. The token can be forwarded through service calls and verified later. A downstream service can verify the first identity in the flow from a trusted cryptographic credential, not just from a caller saying "trust me, this is really Alice." For ordinary synchronous calls, that signed identity can travel with the request. The agent-backed tool might call a service that needs to know the user's current capabilities before returning data. The service mesh asks the authorization data plane to validate the token and resolve the user's current capabilities. The downstream service still owns the final authorization decision: whether this user can view this resource, update it, trigger the operation, or violate some highly opinionated NoPineapplesOnPizzaOrders policy. User Identity Delegation does not decide every service's policy. It gives that service verified user context to evaluate its own policy. Token Exchange Preserves Both Identities Some delegated work does not fit into one short request. An agent may need to continue after the original session has ended, poll for status, update a ticket, prepare a pull request, or perform follow-up work. That work may happen after the original signed-in request has ended, and the software actor doing the work should still act on behalf of the user that started the automation. That is where the token exchange comes in. Figure 2: For work that outlives one request, the token exchange converts the user identity JWT into a delegated token with actor attribution, bounded by the user's consent. The token exchange turns the short-lived user identity token into delegated authority with actor attribution. Depending on the shape of the caller, that exchange can use standard OAuth flows such as OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange for service-to-service flows, Authorization Code with PKCE for user-facing apps, Device Authorization for CLIs and headless tools, and refresh tokens for renewal. It's worth noting that token renewal refreshes require capability and consent validation before completion. The actor is not an LLM deciding to work on its own. It is the workload, application, CLI, or service harness executing the delegated task, tied back to the user-originated command. The shape is intentionally familiar: OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange gives us the language of exchanging one token for another while preserving delegation context. User Identity Delegation uses that pattern in Block's internal environment, where the exchanged token preserves the user identity and records the actor in an act claim anchored in workload identity. In other words, the token can say: this is the user, and this is the software acting on their behalf. That distinction is what makes both auditing and consent enforcement possible. Consent Narrows What Can Be Used The consent control plane records what the user agreed to delegate to that software actor. In the incident response flow, the user might allow the agent-backed tool to read build status, inspect service metadata, or create a draft change, while withholding permission to deploy to production or read unrelated data. This is where the distinction between authority and delegation matters. The control plane is deliberately not the source of truth for what the user can do. Our existing capability grant system remains that. The control plane records the user's intent: which capabilities the user agreed to delegate to this particular actor. It also gives the user a place to view and revoke active delegations. Consent does not create authority. It only narrows authority that already exists and an agent cannot delegate authority they do not possess. That boundary is easy to blur in delegated systems, so User Identity Delegation keeps consent separate from current capability grants. We also restrict which capabilities can be granted and to which types of actors. Consents are only ever a strict subset of a user's capabilities. For example, an incident-response actor might be delegated permission to read build status, inspect service metadata, and create draft changes. Deploying to production, reading unrelated Slack history, or accessing customer-impacting data can remain outside that delegation even if the user has some of those permissions in another context. The Data Plane Computes Effective Authority The authorization data plane enforces all of this at decision time. This is the point where many systems have already lost the thread: the downstream service may not know a user existed at all. When the tool calls the downstream service, the service mesh asks the data plane to validate the token. The data plane verifies the JWT, checks audience and freshness, identifies both the user and the software actor, resolves the user's current capability grants, and computes effective delegated capabilities as the intersection of two sets: Figure 3: Effective delegated capabilities is the intersection of what the user can do now and what they consented to delegate to this actor. The intersection is the core security property. If the user consented to a capability they no longer hold, it drops out because the grant no longer exists. If the user holds a capability but never consented to delegate it to this actor, it drops out because consent does not grant it. If the delegated token has no consent record at all, the effective set is empty. Authority and delegation must both be present. The downstream service still owns its own authorization behavior. User Identity Delegation does not make every service's policy correct. What it provides is a better input: verified user context, actor attribution, and a capability set already clamped to both current authority and delegated consent. A service still has to decide whether the subject, actor, action, resource, and runtime context are acceptable for the operation being attempted. The user, meanwhile, gets a revocation path. Revoking a consent record removes the published consent state used by downstream evaluation. A delegation system that cannot answer "is this still allowed right now?" is just a permission grant wearing a different hat. With those pieces in place, we stop collapsing "the user" and "the tool" into one ambiguous identity for a growing class of flows. What User Identity Delegation Gives Us The pieces above give User Identity Delegation four properties: Identity context is verified cryptographically. Authority is constrained by consent and current grants. Delegation can survive service and workload boundaries. The resulting action is auditable as subject plus actor rather than one ambiguous identity. Now we can give a more precise answer to "who's asking?" In this flow, the answer is not just "the engineer" and not just "the agent." It is this engineer, through this software actor acting on their behalf, with this bounded authority, for this request. From the user's perspective, the model is also easier to reason about: this request came from me, I delegated this actor to do a bounded set of work, and it cannot use more authority than I have right now or more authority than I agreed to delegate. Beyond Agents We accelerated building this system as work with AI agents saw broader adoption. There was a clear need to answer the question posed above across the wide surface of AI users here at Block. But this is one piece of a broader story. Any system that wants to make a request to another service where what is returned depends on what the initiator of the call has access to can use this model. That includes agent-backed tools, internal CLIs, remote build environments, cloud development environments, async jobs, and service-to-service workflows where downstream access depends on the original user. The failure mode is not unique to AI. Broad service identities are tempting anywhere software needs to act for people. They are easy to wire up, but they are hard to reason about later. User Identity Delegation gives us a path that is still ergonomic for developers while preserving the context that downstream systems need. Where We Are Going The destination is still the first-principles model, where effective authority is the intersection of every layer of context available at decision time. Each constraint can only narrow the set, never expand it: Figure 4: Effective authority is the intersection of every layer of context available at decision time; each constraint can only narrow the set, never expand it. We are still extending this model across more of our flows. What is already in place is useful on its own: signed user identity, delegated tokens with actor attribution, consented capability grants, downstream validation, capability intersection, and user-visible revocation. What we are building toward is a richer runtime context: services reasoning not only about which user and which capabilities, but about the origin of the request, the workload doing the work, the action being attempted, the resource being touched, and the assurance level the operation requires. Resource owners should also be able to configure what can never be delegated. Some capabilities should be available only to the user directly, or only through actors that meet stronger requirements. For example, an owner might decide that read-only investigation capabilities can be delegated to an incident-response actor, but administrative capabilities cannot. That future direction follows from what User Identity Delegation has already made clearer: broad service identities and pure user impersonation both remove context that downstream systems need. The model gets stronger as more of that context becomes available at decision time: subject, actor, origin, invocation, resource, action, assurance, and consent. The future version should shrink the need for broad standing service identities, make agent actions easier to explain, and let sensitive operations demand stronger assurance without forcing every workflow into one rigid pattern: powerful automation without super-identities. We have the beginning of the right shape: authority that is delegated explicitly, carried in a verifiable token, constrained by consent and current grants, and visible enough for downstream services to make better decisions. That is already a better answer to "who's asking?"

title: The MBA Doesn't Predict Exit Outcomes
summary: The market knowledge your talent decisions depend on — centralized. Verata unifies company intelligence, executive data, and search management in one platform built for PE talent and executive search.
body_text: The MBA finding has immediate practical implications for how PE firms structure their CEO searches and evaluate candidates: Stop using MBA as a screening filter. If your search specifications include "MBA required" or "MBA strongly preferred," recognize that this criterion eliminates approximately half of all potential CEO candidates while providing no measurable improvement in expected outcomes. The 2.6 percentage point gap is indistinguishable from noise. Do not pay the MBA premium. If your firm systematically pays higher compensation to MBA-holding CEOs based on the assumption that the credential signals higher capability, the data does not support that premium. Compensation should be based on the specific value a CEO is expected to create, not on the brand name of their graduate school. Evaluate skills directly. The MBA teaches a set of skills -- financial analysis, strategic frameworks, organizational management. If those skills are relevant to your portfolio company's specific situation, evaluate them through case-based assessment, reference triangulation, and structured interviews. Do not use the MBA as a shortcut for skills you can and should evaluate directly. Reconsider your pipeline architecture. If your search partners are building candidate slates by starting with MBA alumni databases and then filtering from there, the architecture of your search is biased toward a credential that does not predict outcomes. Start with the operating requirements of the role and work backward to candidates, rather than starting with credentials and hoping they map to capability. The MBA is the most over-indexed credential in PE CEO selection. It tells you where someone came from. It does not tell you whether they will deliver the exit. A rational selection process would weight it accordingly -- which is to say, barely at all.

company_name: Definitive Healthcare Corp. Class A Common Stock
title: Align sales and marketing in healthcare
summary: See how shared healthcare intelligence brings sales and marketing together for greater impact.
body_text: Sales and marketing teams share the same goal—driving growth—but they often rely on different definitions of success and disconnected data to get there. In healthcare, those differences can create blind spots. Without a shared understanding of the landscape, teams can interpret the same markets differently, leading to missed sales opportunities and disconnected campaigns. Read the healthcare leader’s guide to getting teams in lockstep with a single source of truth to learn how shared healthcare intelligence can help commercial teams align strategies, make confident go-to-market decisions, and drive better results. Inside the guide, you’ll see why sales and marketing teams often interpret the same signals through a different lens, and learn how to build a shared data strategy that creates lasting alignment across your organization.

title: Evaluating Newforma Alternatives: A Guide for Architecture and Engineering Firms in 2026
summary: The leading alternatives to Newforma in 2026 are TonicDM, Autodesk Construction Cloud (now renamed Autodesk Forma), and Cogram.
body_text: The leading alternatives to Newforma in 2026 are TonicDM, Autodesk Construction Cloud (now renamed Autodesk Forma), and Cogram. TonicDM is a lean, lower-cost tool for filing project emails and running basic construction administration. Autodesk Construction Cloud fits firms standardizing on Autodesk. Cogram is an AI-native platform built for architects and engineers that keeps project email, correspondence, RFIs and submittals, meeting minutes, field reports, and search in one place. What Newforma does well Newforma helped create the project information management (PIM) category in 2003 and was, for a time, the go-to solution for architecture and engineering firms. Battery Ventures took a majority stake in Newforma in 2017 , and Ethos Capital acquired the company in 2023 . Many design firms we spoke to were clear on what they appreciate in Newforma’s capabilities. Four strengths came up throughout conversations: A defensible record of project email The most common reason firms value Newforma is that if used consistently, it keeps a record of project correspondence, which can be critical if a dispute surfaces years later. One long-time user said: "The biggest thing that I hold tight to with Newforma is the fact that it can maintain email correspondence. We can track our emails, whereas other software is unable to do that well." Another design firm, after more than a decade of using Newforma, confirms the platform’s strength as a system of record in disputes: "I enjoy Newforma. I consider it litigation software for documentation purposes." Search across the project and filesystem access Firms repeatedly named indexing and search as the feature they would most fear losing. Newforma continuously indexes project folders, so staff can dig up an email, an attachment, or a document from years back: "One thing the team loves about Newforma is the indexing.” Firms also appreciate that Newforma overlays an existing file system rather than moving data somewhere new, so people can open project files from inside Newforma without changing how the firm stores anything: "I always love Newforma because it overlays itself over our traditional file system, so we can view the files within the project folder from within the Newforma project. Just the ability to do that is huge." RFI, submittal, and transmittal tracking On the construction administration side, firms rely on Newforma to log and time-stamp who sent what and when. That is both a workflow and a form of protection: "What Newforma does is it allows us to track that. We can log when it's submitted, when it's reviewed, whether it's approved or sent back with revisions. It really helps us keep things on track." "We have to be able to track that and time stamp that, because that's a piece that could really hurt the company. You sent this. We responded. That's a very crucial piece, to have that protection." These Newforma capabilities allow architecture and engineering firms to store project records and make those easily accessible to defend the firm’s work when needed. Why architecture and engineering firms are migrating from Newforma to alternatives Despite these strengths, in 2026, many architecture and engineering firms are looking for alternatives to Newforma, motivated by several factors: The cost structure of Newforma In our conversations with former and current Newforma customers, firms routinely describe paying for license counts several times larger than the number of people who consistently use the tools. Often this is the result of paying for a bundled product, where only some modules see consistent usage and only by a subset of the licensed user base. One Head of Technology at a US design firm put the gap plainly: Of the firm's roughly eighty licenses, about a dozen people used the tools regularly, at more than $500 a license. "Too much for what we don't use." That works out to around $40,000 a year to support a dozen active users, most of whom only touched email filing. Because Newforma is sometimes sold as one bundle rather than by module, firms can't trim down to the parts they rely on. Another firm described their situation as: "Newforma comes as one package. You pay for a lot of these things that you don't get to use, and I don't want to pay for something and then buy something else to replace it." Smaller firms often can't reach a workable number at all, because the seat minimums outstrip their team size. One practice of under twenty people found the minimum was around fifty seats, which made the cost per license "way too high." One firm cut its bill sharply once it measured actual usage against its license total: from roughly $80,000 a year to under $20,000, "based on the numbers and the actual real use.” For most firms, this mismatch only becomes visible at a renewal, or when a new cost-conscious hire pauses to ask how many people are really using what the firm is paying for. The split of Newforma’s legacy product (Project Center) and cloud product (Konekt) Newforma offers both its legacy on-premise product, Project Center, and its cloud product, Konekt. Some firms we spoke with are moving work to Konekt, while others said they expect Newforma to encourage a move over time. Firms described the products as having separate APIs, and several said Konekt does not yet cover every Project Center workflow. This can leave teams split across both: some data and workflows in the cloud, the rest still on-premise, with no clean bridge between them. In our conversations, several firms said this transition was what prompted them to look at alternatives. For firms considering a move, it can be a natural moment to ask whether the destination should still be Newforma. One large architecture practice reported: "There are many things we do in the legacy version of Newforma that don't exist in the cloud yet... my gut is telling me they're gonna force us into [the migration] sometime." A perceived slowness of development In our conversations, firms repeatedly described Newforma as a product that no longer innovates quickly, in a time where technology is going through a fundamental shift with AI and firms expect their software to take real work off their plate. Newforma’s core dates to the mid-2000s. To the people using it, it still looks and behaves that way. One engineering firm said: "The entire system is legacy. It's not built with AI in mind, so any AI they use is like an add-on." Some connect the stall in R&D to ownership: after two private equity owners since 2017, some customers read the priority as protecting revenue rather than building. Newforma is working on a cloud successor, but some firms we spoke with describe the pace as slow and the roadmap as always a year out. Alternatives to Newforma in 2026 Over the last decade, several alternatives to Newforma have emerged. We cover the leading three, TonicDM, Cogram, and ACC in detail below. The table below compares the leading Newforma alternatives on the jobs architecture and engineering firms care about. The figures come from firms we spoke with and each vendor's published materials. Capability Newforma TonicDM ACC Cogram Best for Established A/E system of record Lean, low-cost email and basic CA Firms consolidating on Autodesk; model coordination AI-native A/E system of record Project email of record Yes, its core strength Yes Not built for it; usually paired with a separate tool Yes, can file project email automatically with AI RFIs, submittals, transmittals Yes, deep Narrower CA tier Yes (Autodesk Docs and Build) Yes, with AI-assisted triage Field reports and punch lists Yes No Limited Yes, dedicated mobile capture Meeting minutes Yes No No Yes, AI notetaker AI (search, filing, agents) Add-on, cloud only Limited Limited Built in from the ground up On-prem or customer-controlled storage Yes (Project Center) Cloud only Cloud only Yes: your cloud or your own file system Works alongside Procore and ACC Yes Limited Native to Autodesk Yes. Two-way Procore sync; connects to ACC Pricing model Track-based or bundle Per user Per user; collaborators need Autodesk seats Modular, floating licenses, free viewers Reported cost signal About $500 per seat per year About $15 per user per month, roughly a third of Newforma Pricey per seat for design firms Pay only for the modules and seats you use TonicDM TonicDM is a cloud platform built for architecture and engineering firms, founded by an ex-Gensler technologist who had used Newforma Project Center, so the Newforma-alternative positioning is baked into its origin. Tonic covers the core PIM jobs: email filing, file sharing, transmittals with download tracking, and search across one or many projects, with an optional construction-administration tier for RFIs and submittals. It is priced per user, around $15 per user per month, and firms consistently report it runs about a third of what they paid for Newforma. In a 2024 review, AECbytes named Lake|Flato as a firm that moved from Newforma to Tonic. What users like is that it is lean and fast. On the 4specs forum, an architect who moved his firm off Newforma in 2023 put the trade-off plainly: "Tonic was 1/3rd of the price, and granted, it's half the program Newforma is, but what it does, it does much better than Newforma does." They also said adoption climbed once his staff were on it: "I had maybe 50% success ratio with Newforma, but a much higher utilization ratio with Tonic, probably over 90% or higher. It's just easier to use, and much, much faster performing." The flip side to this is scope. Tonic deliberately does less: its construction-administration depth is narrower than Newforma's, and it does not offer field reports, a mobile app, or punch lists. For a firm that wants a lighter, cheaper, easier email-and-CA record and nothing more, that focus is the appeal. For a firm that also wants field reports, meeting minutes, or AI working across its project data, Tonic leaves gaps. Autodesk Construction Cloud Autodesk Construction Cloud (ACC) is a contender for firms that want to consolidate on Autodesk. Its modules, Autodesk Docs and Build, cover document control, a common data environment, and construction-administration workflows like RFIs and submittals, and it connects tightly to Revit. In 2026 Autodesk began renaming ACC to Autodesk Forma, and Autodesk Docs to Forma Data Management. ACC is especially strong for model-based collaboration: architects and engineers praise it for hosting and sharing Revit models, running clash detection, and keeping drawings in one controlled place. As one architect put it in a review : "It offers better co-ordination tools for designers, and makes full use of rendering tools to be able to fly through models to identify clashes." ACC is priced per user, and collaborators generally need their own paid Autodesk seat , or consume one of yours, to take part. Practitioners are blunt about this on Autodesk's own forums : "It doesn't make any sense to me that everyone would need a license to receive a submittal or an RFI." That model is expensive for design firms that coordinate with consultants, owners, and contractors who will not all buy Autodesk licenses. Design-side reviewers echo it plainly: "it is pricey per seat," "its cost is very high." Finally, ACC is not built to be a project email system. Architects and engineers consistently pair it with a separate tool for filing and archiving project correspondence, which is the job tools like Newforma, Cogram, and TonicDM are built around. If email-of-record is central to how your firm defends its work, ACC alone does not cover it. Cogram: Founded in 2021, Cogram matches the breadth of Newforma's project record with a faster, AI-native interface. It is built around AI to remove the manual, repetitive admin work that slows project teams down. We examine the platform in detail in the next section. Cogram: an AI-native alternative to Newforma Cogram makes AI software specifically for architects and engineers. The Cogram platform is a suite of tools for project management, with modules including: Email Management Instead of manual drag-and-drop filing, AI summarizes incoming and outgoing email and files a copy of each project email to the right project folder. Email that has been filed receives a tag in Outlook to indicate filing status. Send large files with an audit log, and manage transmittals. Contract Administration Manage RFIs, Submittals, Change Orders, and more in one place. Receiving and issuing works with Procore and via Outlook. Initial triage and review against specs is AI-assisted. Meeting Minutes Cogram’s notetaker for virtual meetings (Teams, Zoom, Webex, Google) and in-person meetings automates minutes in your firm’s custom templates. Controls built for the architecture and engineering industry mean attendance in meetings and sharing of minutes can be carefully managed. Field Automates data capture for field reports, punch lists, or surveys via transcription and photo capture in Cogram’s mobile app. Also provides tools for drawing management and data access in the field. Agent and Search Chat with your project record and quickly find anything across projects. Firms use Cogram’s Agent workbench to set up long-running agents for regular project reporting, QA/QC, or task management. Project Management Task management, scheduling, and collaboration. Integrates with tools like Deltek, Unanet, and Teams. Modular pricing and floating licenses: Each module in Cogram can be purchased separately, and license counts for multiple modules can be independent, so architecture and engineering firms only pay for what they need. Usage analytics are transparently shared in Cogram’s administration dashboard. Licenses in Cogram are floating. That means customers can deactivate a license at any time and reassign the free license to someone else in the organization. Viewer licenses in Cogram are free, so anyone in the organization can sign in, find and view information, or respond to assignments. That licensing flexibility and cost structure makes Cogram work for organizations ranging from small teams to the largest design firms in the world, across more than 80 customers. Many of those organizations started out with one or two of Cogram’s capabilities and over time have layered on additional modules. Several have made a complete transition from a legacy PIM software like Newforma to the Cogram platform. Integrations: Deltek and Unanet: Cogram integrates with Deltek Vantagepoint, Ajera, Vision, and Unanet for project provisioning, member management, and close-out: when projects are created in Deltek those appear automatically in Cogram. When projects are closed out in Deltek they automatically close out in Cogram. Procore: For projects where design firms work with contractors that use Procore, Cogram’s Procore connector allows RFIs and submittals to be managed from within Cogram. Correspondence created or updated in Procore is synced into Cogram. Review, forwarding, and issuing can be done entirely in Cogram and responses are synced back into Procore. All data synced into Cogram is stored and backed up, so design firms have their own copy of the record outside of Procore. Microsoft Teams: Search Teams channels from Cogram with AI, or talk to Cogram’s Agent from project channels in Teams Sharepoint: Search and work with files from Sharepoint, directly in Cogram Autodesk Construction Cloud: Search and work with files from ACC, directly in Cogram File systems: Cogram’s filesystem connector makes your file system searchable from Cogram, allowing staff to access and save files directly to your storage. We explore this in more detail below. A platform that works with the cloud and on-prem file systems: Cogram can be used both with Cogram-hosted cloud storage of project information, or with customer-controlled storage. The platform is architected to support both those firms that are cloud-native and those that value a long-term on-premise or hybrid storage approach. In the case of customer-controlled storage, two options are available: Cogram can store all project information in the customer’s cloud storage, or directly in the customer’s file system. Integrations are available with systems like Panzura, LucidLink, Nasuni, Egnyte, and others. In the case of Cogram-hosted storage, customers can use Cogram’s API to export their full project record at any time, in a well-structured, file-based export format. That export capability can also be used to regularly sync the project record to your firm’s own storage or archival environment, so a current copy of the record always sits in storage you control. Controls, Security, and Data Export: Cogram does not train AI models on customer data and is SOC 2 Type II-certified. An overview of Cogram’s security and control posture is available at https://cogram.com/security . Authentication is via SSO or two-factor sign-in. Support for Microsoft Entra (Active Directory) makes authentication and access manageable at scale. Migrating from Newforma to Cogram The hardest part of leaving Newforma is usually the migration itself. Firms have years of project email and records they cannot afford to lose. How the move works depends on where you want your project record to live, and Cogram supports two models. Option A: cloud storage If you want Cogram to hold your record in the cloud, Cogram imports your historical Newforma project email and correspondence into the Cogram platform, mapped to the right projects, so past records stay searchable from day one. Projects in Cogram can come from Unanet, Deltek, or another tool. Cogram runs the migration as a shared project with named owners on both sides and a live tracker. A typical import takes about two weeks once your project list and source access are in place, moving through five phases: scoping which projects to bring over, securely extracting the data, importing and validating it, reconciling the results with you, then cutting over with training. Your Newforma source data is only read, never changed, and is handled in a secure environment Cogram removes once you sign off. Option B: file system storage If you want to keep your project record in your own file system, as many firms did with Newforma, the migration is lighter as Newforma already stores your records on your file server. The Cogram Connector, a lightweight Windows service, connects to your file system in place, indexes your project folders so your history is searchable in Cogram from the start, and files new email and correspondence into the right folders going forward. Your files stay where they are, under your control. The connector talks to Cogram outbound-only over TLS, so there are no inbound ports to open and no firewall changes, your content stays on your network, and access is trimmed per user so each person only sees files their existing Windows permissions already allow. With either option, you review sample projects and give final acceptance before anything goes live, with a dedicated account lead, migration engineer, and customer success contact working with you throughout. A migration can also run alongside going live, or on its own timeline afterward, so your teams can start using Cogram without waiting for every historical project to move. Next Steps If you’d like to discuss a migration from Newforma to Cogram, the team at Cogram is happy to help you evaluate options. To get started, book a migration assessment . If you do decide to make the move, we’ll run it as a high-touch process so your firm’s project delivery stays uninterrupted. We’re also happy to connect you with other design firms that have made the move. FAQs What are the best alternatives to Newforma in 2026? The main alternatives are TonicDM, Cogram, and Autodesk Construction Cloud. TonicDM is a lean, lower-cost cloud tool for email filing and basic construction administration. Autodesk Construction Cloud suits firms consolidating on Autodesk. Cogram is an AI-native platform built for architects and engineers, covering email, correspondence, meeting minutes, field reports, and search in one place. The right choice depends on whether you want the lightest possible tool, deeper Autodesk integration, or a modern system of record with AI built in. What is the difference between Newforma Project Center and Newforma Konekt? Project Center is Newforma's legacy on-premise product, installed and maintained on your own servers. Konekt is its newer cloud product. Some firms we spoke with are moving work to Konekt, while others said they expect Newforma to encourage a move over time. Firms mid-transition tell us Konekt does not yet match every Project Center feature, so they often run part of their work in the cloud and part on-premise. Is Newforma being discontinued? No. Newforma is still sold and supported. Customers can migrate from Newforma Project Center, its legacy on-premise product, to its cloud product, Konekt, which firms tell us is still catching up on features. Some firms treat that transition as a moment to re-evaluate whether Newforma is still the right platform. Does Newforma have AI? Yes. Newforma has announced AI capabilities, including natural-language search, submittal review, and email filing, as part of its Konekt cloud product. Per Newforma's own materials, these are cloud features, so a firm on the on-premise Project Center would move to the cloud to use them. How much does Newforma cost? Newforma does not publish pricing, but firms we spoke with report paying around $500 per user per year, and that it is sometimes sold as a bundle rather than by module, with seat minimums, so smaller firms and firms with light usage often pay for far more than they use. One firm told us it held around eighty licenses but had only about a dozen regular users. Is there a cheaper alternative to Newforma? Yes. TonicDM is reported to cost about a third of Newforma. Cogram uses modular pricing with floating licenses, so you pay only for the modules and the number of seats you actually use, and viewer access is free. Some firms found they were overpaying: one told us they cut their Newforma spend by more than three quarters once they matched licenses to real usage. Is Autodesk Construction Cloud or Procore a good Newforma replacement for architects and engineers? They can be, but design firms often find both are oriented to the general contractor's workflow rather than the design side. On a project the contractor owns, the architect or engineer works inside someone else's system and someone else's record. Autodesk Construction Cloud is also priced per user, and collaborators generally need their own paid Autodesk seat, which gets expensive for design firms coordinating with consultants and owners. Neither is designed primarily as a project email system, which is why design firms usually keep a separate system of record. Can I keep my historical Newforma emails and project data if I switch? Yes. Newforma's on-premise Project Center keeps your records on your own file server, so that data is yours to bring. You can import your historical project email and correspondence into a new platform, or, if you keep your own file system, connect to it in place so the history stays searchable without a bulk move. How long does it take to migrate off Newforma? A typical cloud import takes about two weeks once your project list and source access are in place. It runs in five phases: scoping the projects, extracting the data, importing and validating it, reconciling the results with you, and cutting over with training. If you keep your own file system, the migration is lighter. Can you run Newforma and a replacement at the same time? Yes, and many firms do. New projects start on the new platform while in-flight projects finish on Newforma with a reduced seat count. The two systems do not interfere, so you can move at a pace that protects live project delivery. What should we test before switching from Newforma? Test three things: run search on your own historical data and see whether the new system finds what you need. Export your record yourself and open it, to confirm you can leave with your data intact. And track filing adoption during a pilot, since a record is only as good as what actually gets filed. Does Cogram integrate with Procore, Deltek, Autodesk Construction Cloud, and Bluebeam? Yes. Cogram syncs RFIs and submittals two ways with Procore and keeps your own copy of the record. It integrates with Deltek (Vantagepoint, Ajera, and Vision) and Unanet for project setup and close-out, and connects to Autodesk Construction Cloud, SharePoint, Microsoft Teams, and your file system for search and file access. Cogram’s API covers anything not listed. How do I export data from Newforma Project Center? If you run Project Center on-premise, your project records and filed email already live on your own file server, organized in your project folders, so there is no vendor export to request: the data is yours to read in place. A migration works by reading those folders and that filed email from the source, never changing them. If you are evaluating a move, a migration assessment can scope which projects and how much history to bring across. title: Another 5 “Bad” Cars I Want Anyway
summary: At this point, now 15 cars and three installments into this exercise in aspirational automotive masochism, it might seem like cars with bad reputations are my real passion. That’s not strictly true, but my interest in the unfortunate certainly runs deep and it is beyond redemption, as these next five picks clearly attest: 2005–08 Jaguar […]
body_text: At this point, now 15 cars and three installments into this exercise in aspirational automotive masochism, it might seem like cars with bad reputations are my real passion. That’s not strictly true, but my interest in the unfortunate certainly runs deep and it is beyond redemption, as these next five picks clearly attest: 2005–08 Jaguar X-Type Sportwagon Historics Auctioneers What it is: The X-type was Jaguar’s first real attempt to field a competitor to the BMW 3-Series in the lucrative, European compact near-luxury sedan segment. Ford, Jaguar’s then-patron, unfortunately didn’t learn from GM’s mistakes with the Cadillac Cimarron in the 1980s. What the Blue Oval served up was essentially a warmed-over Ford Mondeo. And instead of following BMW’s lead by offering the X-Type in sedan, coupe and convertible body styles, which the market wanted at the time, Jaguar inexplicably gave buyers the choice of just sedan or wagon. While the sedan is a bit frumpy, the 3.0-liter V-6 long-roof or “Sportwagon” is genuinely quite handsome. And genuinely rare, with most sources quoting under 4500 total built and about 1600 sent here to the U.S. What makes it bad: The X-type simply wasn’t convincing as a Jaguar. Its Ford Mondeo-ness oozed out of every crevice and not even real walnut veneer and nice leather could compensate for the Ford parts bin bits that were everywhere. Cooling system and electrical issues, plus fragile AWD transfer cases soured the car’s reputation and it was simply never an aspirational car for younger buyers in the way that a 3-Series was. Why I want one: This is simple. I love rare, oddball cars, especially when they’re wagons. When those things intersect in the Venn diagram of not-great cars, well, good luck keeping me off Facebook Marketplace. The wagon really is attractive. Especially in a dark color, and minus the leaper on the hood, it’s a real looker. Sadly, while the sedan was offered in the U.S. with a manual, the wagon wasn’t. No matter, I know where there’s a clean-looking wagon and a t-boned manual sedan, and you know where I’m going from there—the stick shift, Joe Dirt shooting brake of my dreams. 2006–07 Chevrolet Malibu Maxx SS Chevrolet What it is: The Malibu Maxx is one of the weirdest GM midsize sedans ever. Not quite a wagon, and therefore sort of a hatchback, the car managed to combine the two body styles most heartily disliked by the American car buyers of the early 2000s. Still, it was practical, and not at all bad to drive in SS trim with its 3.9-liter LZ9 V-6 that made about 240 horsepower, 18” wheels, and firmer suspension. What makes it bad: The sixth-generation Malibu was about a decade behind nearly everyone else in terms of fit, finish, and materials. The interior plastics and switchgear in particular were low points. Frankly, the car is also just plain weird, and “weird” rarely translates to success in the new car market. Why I want one: As maybe the last truly weird GM car ever, the Malibu Maxx SS is actually an historically significant car. Maybe it’s not Corvair – or SSR -level strange, but it’s an iconoclast’s automobile to be sure. Just 2600 were built and while I have no idea how many survive, I can’t remember the last time I saw one in the wild. There are none that I can find currently for sale, but when one does pop up, it probably won’t be pricey. 2004–06 Volkswagen Phaeton Volkswagen What it is: The Phaeton was VW’s attempt to produce an ultra-luxury executive sedan to compete with BMW and Mercedes-Benz. It was the most visible manifestation of VW Group chair Ferdinand Piëch’s most active phase in trying to take Volkswagen upmarket. With either a 4.2-liter V-8 or 6.0-liter W-12 to choose from, the Phaeton shared a fair bit with the Bentley Continental GT and Flying Spur … including their knee-capping maintenance costs. What makes it bad: The Germans have a reputation for over-engineering, and the Phaeton was certainly the King Tiger tank of VWs. But instead of breaking down in far off places like the Ardennes Forest, the Phaeton would be perfectly happy to break something in a driveway near you. Particularly in W-12 form, the car quickly gained a reputation for being absolute hell to work on. Partial disassembly was routine for even the simplest jobs in the engine compartment. When warranties expired, depreciation was vicious. Why I want one: From the minute it was announced, I was utterly fascinated by the VW Group’s new W-12 engine, and while I find a Bentley way too pretentious for my preferences, a W-12-powered VW sedan that sold for the equivalent of about $160,000 in today’s money? Sign me up. At the prices they’re selling for now, (under 10 grand for one with some miles, or mid-teens for a really clean one), I can get the whole W-12 thing out of my system once and for all without posing an immediate Chapter 7 risk. There’s even a guy out there who makes very cool coffee tables out of dead W-12 blocks. So, there’s that for a plan B, I suppose. 1991–92 Lotus Elan M100 Lotus What it was: By the early 1990s, a large chunk of Lotus’ model range (namely, the Eclat /Excel) had run its course, and the company was left with only the aging Esprit to flog. Lotus desperately needed an entry-level car, and it fielded one with some help from GM, its corporate parent at the time. Peter Stevens, who did the first facelift of the Esprit, designed a car that Richard Hammond of Top Gear remarked was oddly square, seemingly as wide as it was long. But for driving purists, the real heresy came from the fact that this Lotus was front-wheel drive. What makes it bad: Although the Elan M100 was true to the Lotus ethos in that it was relatively lightweight, and it utilized a fiberglass body over a backbone chassis, testers couldn’t get over its FWD architecture, even though the handling was peerless (albeit too docile to some). Mate the odd looks to a somewhat anemic Isuzu four-cylinder and the usual Lotus idiosyncrasies, and you have a car that gets very little love beyond the few thousand owners who do reportedly adore their cars. Then there’s the fact that, at the same time, Mazda debuted the original MX-5 Miata . Ironically, the Japanese borrowed a lot of the Miata’s design philosophy from the original 1960s Lotus Elan , and unlike the “new” Elan M100, the more conventional Mazda became a massive success. Why I want one: It goes without saying that the M100 Elan is cheap. They rarely break $20,000, and they really are entertaining to drive and strikingly weird to look at, all while being somewhat less of a headache than a Lotus of the 1970s. A ringing endorsement, no? 1971–73 Triumph Stag Mecum What it was: The Stag was British Leyland’s attempt to field a cheaper alternative to the Mercedes-Benz 350SL . Amazingly, Triumph almost succeeded, narrowly snatching defeat from the jaws of victory. In terms of styling, the Stag had it, courtesy of Italian Giovanni Michelotti. Just like the Benz, it had a SOHC V-8 with aluminum heads. The wood-trimmed interior and removable hardtop were also very Benz-like, as was the automatic gearbox (although a four-speed with overdrive was available). Unlike the Benz, the Stag also had a pair of usable back seats. What makes it bad: Well, it was 1970s British Leyland, and in addition to the usual dodgy electrics by Lord Voldemort, there was the engine—the slightest bit of overheating (to which the cars were naturally prone) could warp those lovely aluminum heads. And if you managed to not boil the engine, well, there was always the danger of catastrophic timing chain failure lurking around every corner. Much of this was eventually sorted out for U.K. customers, but the Stag skulked out of the U.S. market awash in claims on its paltry 12-month/12,000-mile warranty. Why I want one: I’ve always thought the Stag was a really handsome car, especially with the hardtop in place. The 3.0-liter V-8 sounds delicious, and it’s especially nice paired with the four-speed, plus electric overdrive manual box. It’s a rare combination of Italian style, V-8 burble, a manual box, and affordability. Decent ones can be had in the teens, and really nice ones don’t stretch much past 20 grand. Unlike the newer cars on the list, it’s fairly DIY friendly, and I’m told that there are fixes for the maladies that skewered the car in the U.S. 50 year ago, or you can just do an engine swap (a similarly sized Rover V-8 is the most popular) as many Stag owners have. The post Another 5 “Bad” Cars I Want Anyway appeared first on Hagerty Media .

In this quarterly Oracle Critical Patch Update, Oracle E-Business Suite received the highest number of patches, 410, constituting about 28% of the total patches released. 1235 of the 1449 (about 86%) security patches in the July Critical Patch Update are for non-Oracle CVEs, such as open-source components included in, and exploitable within, Oracle product distributions. title: Foundation models come to tables and time series
summary: Most of the conversations about foundation models are related to language and images. Less discussed, but more consequential for a bank, is that the same idea is applied to one of the most widely used forms of data: rows in a table.
body_text: Communications Santander CEST Linkedin Instagram X Most of the conversations about foundation models are related to language and images. Less discussed, but more consequential for a bank, is that the same idea is now being applied to one of the most widely used forms of data: rows in a table and numbers over time. Over the past year, pretrained models for this data have matured to the point where they are worth taking seriously in production, and Santander teams are already putting them to the test. Instead of building a forecasting model from scratch for a specific series, Santander took a model that had never seen the data before and asked it to forecast what would happen next (no training step, just a prediction). Pedro Martin, Santander AI Scientist, explains that “time-series foundation models reduce the need to build and maintain separate models, such as ARIMA, SARIMAX or Prophet, for every forecasting use case. By reusing patterns learned from large and diverse datasets, they can produce strong forecasts without fine-tuning, reducing development costs, accelerating deployment and enabling deployment across thousands of client (or product) level series. Potential applications include forecasting balances, transaction volumes and liquidity”. Train once, reapply on demand A traditional forecasting model is trained on one series, such as daily card transactions for a given product, and learns that series alone. A time-series foundation model is trained once, on an enormous and varied collection of series, and can then forecast a series it has never seen before, with no additional training. This is called zero-shot forecasting, and a year ago it sounded implausible. The current generation makes it credible. Google's TimesFM was pretrained on roughly one hundred billion time points. Amazon's Chronos-2 (late 2025) tokenises a series and passes it through a transformer, handling not just one series but many related ones and external drivers at once. TabPFN-TS, from Prior Labs, reaches state-of-the-art forecasts with only about eleven million parameters and was pretrained entirely on synthetic data. Using one of these looks less like machine learning and more like calling a function: from chronos import ChronosPipeline pipe = ChronosPipeline.from_pretrained("amazon/chronos-2") forecast = pipe.predict(context=recent_history, horizon=30) # no training step Raising the bar In a bank, there are thousands of series to forecast (by product, segment, branch and currency) and many are short, sparse or new: precisely the kind of cold-start cases in which a model built from scratch struggles and a pretrained one shines. The same models give strong out-of-the-box baselines for anomaly detection, and a fast baseline is valuable because it tells you whether a bespoke model is actually earning its complexity. On the tabular side, foundation models such as TabPFN are beginning to do the same for classification on the structured data that makes up most of our world. None of this makes classical methods obsolete. A well-specified statistical model, or a gradient-boosted tree tuned to a problem we understand, still often wins, especially where the series has strong, known structure. The honest posture is to treat a foundation model as a strong, cheap starting point and a benchmark to beat, not as an automatic upgrade. In a regulated institution, a model that produces a number that feeds a decision is not merely a convenience. It is something that must be validated, explained and governed. Foundation models raise the bar here, because their internals are harder to interpret, and because using a pretrained model is not, by itself, an account of why a forecast can be trusted. Evolving model-risk expectations across the industry apply to these systems just as they do to any other model. The approach, therefore, is both practical and cautious: they can compress weeks of work into an afternoon, and that speed only creates value if the results are measured against a meaningful baseline, the model’s failure modes are understood and a human remains accountable for the decision it informs. Used that way, the arrival of foundation models in tables and time series is not a threat to careful analytics. It is a faster way to produce an initial analytical baseline. Title: Foundation models come to tables and time series.

title: Altamur cement plant construction to advance
summary: Altamur cement plant construction to advance
body_text: Afghanistan: Deputy governor Sheikh Enamullah Salahuddin has met with Tariq Mahmood, the CEO of Sako Afghan, and the contractor overseeing the Altamur cement mine, alongside officials from the Provincial Directorate of Mines and Petroleum, to review the project's advancement. Representatives from Sako Afghan confirmed that the exploration phase and preliminary development, amounting to US$455,000, have been completed. They also said that construction will begin within the coming days. The company reported that the plant's construction will be finalised within an 18-month timeline, after which full-scale commercial production will commence. Situated in the Altamur district of central Logar Province, the plant will have a production capacity of ~0.8Mt/yr/day of cement.
